RACE WAR ON WARSHIPS.
Negroes in the Crews Tormented by the White Sailors.
[BY TELEGRAPH TO THE TRIBUNE.] Harbor. Me July 20—The race

Bar Harbor, Me., July 20.—The race feeling which exists in the navy against the colored men has been cropping out here since the fleet of seven United States warships arrived. The white sailors have been making it unpleasant for the negroes, and the latter have kept aboard most of the time rather than risk abuse in the streets.

Last Saturday night a number of them came ashore. About midnight several "jackies" got into the tent which the naval branch of the Young Men's Christian Association has erected in the town park, and drove out the negroes who were there for a night's lodging.

Two black sailors were knocked down in Mainst. by a crowd of "jackies," and, after getting a few kicks and punches, scrambled to their feet and ran. One negro was thrown over a board fence into the street. Another found his way to the police station, and was locked up to keep him away from the angry sailors who had been chasing him. Still another rushed into a drug store, and was put into the cellar to avoid the mob. He had to make his way across yards after he went out a back door. Since Saturday night there have been no colored men ashore after dark.

UNCLE SAM'S JACKIES DON'T LIKE NEGROES
BAR HARBOR, Me., July 21.—In the crews of the seven warships now in this harbor are seven negroes, and their white fellow sailors have shown the same race prejudice which other sailors feel. Some of the negro men came ashore last Saturday night and before long there were numerous fights in the streets between white and black sailors. Several whites got into the tent which the naval branch of the Young Men's Christian Association has erected on the town lot and drove out the negroes who had gone there for a night's lodging. Two negroes were knocked down in Main Street. Another was thrown over a board fence and back again.

JACKIES' RACE WAR
Black and White Sailors on Shore Leave Have Trouble.
New York Sun Special Service.
Bar Harbor, Maine, July

New York Sun Special Service.

Bar Harbor, Maine, July 21.—There have been several manifestations of a race war between the black and white sailors of the crews of the several United States warships in the harbor. About midnight last night a number of whites rushed the negroes from the Y. M. C. A. tent, where they were lodging. Later on one negro rushed into the police station and another into a drug store and begged for protection from white jackies who were chasing them. It was reported last night that shore leave would not in future be granted the negroes so as to avoid clashes in the streets.

THE drawing of a color line in the navy may have serious results. A few weeks ago open warfare took place between the white and negro sailors on a United States war vessel. The fracas took place not on the ship, but ashore at Bar Harbor, where the white sailors chased the negro sailors belonging to the same ship and beat many of them severely. On one of the ships a colored seaman was made petty officer and the other petty officers refused to mess with him. The navy department will not, of course, recognize the right of white sailors to proscribe the colored ones. The President is bent upon keeping all the doors of hope wide open to the negro man. But, nevertheless, the President will find this a different proposition from closing a southern postoffice or appointing negroes to high official positions in the south. The inducements held out to get men to enlist in the navy are not brilliant nor alluring, and there has been from time to time difficulty in obtaining the requisite number of blue-jackets. There is no law in this country for the impressment of sailors, and it is not likely that congress would ever enact such a law in time of peace, even if it has the power to do so. Therefore the navy is dependent upon voluntary enlistments, and if the race feeling is to continue white men finding that they have to associate upon equal social terms with negroes in the close quarters of a ship at sea may refuse to enlist. Then, in such a case, the President may find himself face to face with this proposition—either close the door of hope in the navy to the negro, or else to undertake to have the sailors and marines of the navy an exclusively negro force. With such an alternative, it seems more than probable that the "doors of hope" would close.

There are now, and have been all along, for many years, negro sailors in the navy, but no petty officers, we believe, until now. In the forecastle there has never been any acute trouble between the races, except, perhaps, a fracas from time to time. This afternoon about 2 o'clock there was excitement and plenty of it along the river front. The occasion was the sight of a negro struggling in the water near the south bank of the river while five or six young white men were standing on the bank threatening to cut his throat at the same time brandishing a razor before his eyes.

The negro who fortunately caught on some limbs of a tree tells one story while another is gleaned from parties who were in that vicinity, but who declare they were not eye witnesses to the affair. The negro's name is Will Baker. He is a strapping six-footer and says that he was coming up the river in his boat when he noticed six white men on the bank shooting craps. He was watching the game when one of the men asked him if he didn't have some money. He pulled $3 out of his pocket and he claims the young white men set upon him and after taking his money away from him struck him with a stick and threw him into the river. One of the young men had a razor and kept threatening to cut his throat.

The story that is most credited is that the negro came along and asked to be allowed to get in the game. This was at first refused, but finally he was allowed to come in and having a streak of luck won all the money from the white men. They then demanded that he give it up and upon his refusal he was set upon and the money taken away from him. Then fearing that such an act might get them in trouble they threw him in the river and would possibly have killed him had they not been frightened away.

Where the affair occurred has of late been made a rendezvous for crap shooters. Today several of the employes of the Estelle cotton mills took a day off and went across the river for a sort of picnic. Four young men were arrested at the ball park, but the negro who suffered violence says they were not in the crowd. The names of the other six are known to the authorities and they will perhaps be rounded up.

charles-smith-washington-1903-11-13.A1:
HELD UP A CASHIER

Charles Smith Robbed the Treasury Cafe.

AN EXCITING CHASE

SHOT AT HIS PURSUERS AND WOUNDED AN OFFICER.

Threats of Lynching Made — Prisoner Held by Judge Scott for a Hearing Next Week.
Charles Smith, a nineteen-year-old colored boy, held up Philip E. Steuart, the cashier of the Treasury Cafe, at 1400 G street, last night about 8:30 o'clock, robbing him of $28, and shot two street-crossing policemen who joined in chasing him. The crowd that collected was an angry one, and demands for lynching were made by some. George W. Osburn, one of the officers, received a compound fracture of the left leg, and is in the Emergency Hospital. C. M. Edwards, the other officer, escaped serious injury. A bullet from the weapon of the colored man struck him almost directly over the heart, but only broke the skin.

Smith was recently discharged from the Treasury Cafe, where he was employed as dishwasher. He knew that it was the custom of the cashier to leave the cafe after all the waiters and other help had departed, and was also aware that Steuart carried the money away with him. It was about 8:30 o'clock when Steuart was ready to lock the front door to go home. Mr. J. H. Bowling, the proprietor, was not there at the time. Steuart went to the kitchen to see that the cook had securely fastened the rear of the premises. While he was there he heard the front door opened. Returning to the cafe, he was confronted by a colored man, who had made a mask of a napkin. The napkin Smith had taken from the lunch room during the time of his employment there, and had been using it as a handkerchief. It proved a good mask, but the colored highwayman was not able to disguise his voice.

Pointing a revolver at the cashier he cried: "I want your money."

Steuart pushed the weapon aside, but Smith was persistent, and the cashier was forced to hand over to him the money. Putting the loot in his pocket Smith ran from the place toward 15th street. Close behind him Steuart followed, blowing a police whistle.

An Exciting Chase.

His vigorous blowing attracted policemen and others from all directions, and the fleeing colored man had little chance of escaping.

He ran north on 15th street and doubled east on New York avenue. Crossing Policeman Osburn, stationed at 15th and G streets, was the first to join in the chase. A number of pedestrians took part in the pursuit. Just before Smith reached the Oxford Hotel he turned and fired. He missed and fired again. It is thought that he intended the bullet for the citizen members of the pursuing party, but it struck Osburn in the leg and he fell. He pluckily arose and tried to resume the chase, but couldn't stand. Officer Edwards, who was stationed at 14th street and New York avenue, made a dash for the colored boy, who ran into an alley in rear of the hotel. Edwards followed him into the alley, when Smith fired again. The bullet was prevented from doing injury by striking against the note book and a copy of The Evening Star in Edwards' pocket.

Smith had no more bullets in his weapon and was unable to offer further resistance.

Threats of Lynching.

"Kill him," and Lynch him," shouted the crowd. Several policemen in uniform had reached the scene by this time, and some of them, it is stated, took part in the rough handling of the prisoner. The excited crowd would undoubtedly have done him serious harm had not the police surrounded the prisoner and kept the crowd back. Smith was hurried to a cell at the first precinct station, where he was fully identified as the robber of Steuart and where he was relieved of the proceeds of the crime, which he had been too much excited and frightened to throw away. He was nervous and excited, and was afraid he might be taken out by the crowd and given further rough treatment. He had received a few cuts and bruises.

At the hospital it was found that Osburn's injury was considerable, and he will have to remain under treatment several weeks at least. Edwards was not much hurt.

Commissioner Macfarland this morning called on Policeman Osburn and asked after the condition of the injured officer. Mr. Macfarland offered his assistance in case it was needed.

The prisoner was taken to police headquarters this morning and measured and photographed for the gallery. Before being taken there he admitted that he had smashed the big plate glass window at The Hub about three weeks ago and stolen a rain coat and hat. Precinct Detective Clifford Grant heard his confession. The stolen articles were recovered.

Smith Arraigned and Held.

Smith was taken before Judge Scott of the United States branch of the Police Court shortly after 11 o'clock this morning and he was arraigned and given a preliminary hearing on a charge of intent to kill Crossing Policeman Osburn and highway robbery. He was also arraigned on a charge of housebreaking for breaking into the show window of The Hub, at the corner of 14th street and Pennsylvania avenue northwest, October 26 last. Smith was not represented by counsel, and he nervously answered not guilty to each of the charges. Hearing in the case of housebreaking was postponed until Tuesday of next week.

Cashier Steuart testified that he was standing in the rear of the cafe near the door leading into the kitchen when Smith entered last night.

"He started behind the counter, and I asked him where he was going," the witness testified, "and without making any reply he came back to where I was standing and shoved a revolver up in my face and demanded money. I told him that I had none, and with that brushed the revolver aside, but he pointed it in my face again and demanded the money, whereupon I gave him the paper money.

"He said that was not all the money, but I told him that it was, but he insisted that there was more, so I gave him the silver money."

Steuart said that Smith then ran out of the place and down the street, he following behind, blowing a police whistle. Policeman Osburn answered the call and gave chase, but Smith turned around and fired two shots at the officer, the second one causing him to fall to the sidewalk.

Policeman Edwards also gave testimony, stating that he heard two pistol shots and saw a man fall down when the second shot was fired. He said that Smith fired at him, the bullet striking him on the left side, a short distance below the heart, penetrating his clothes. The force of the leaden missile, he said, was broken by hitting against a copy of The Star which he had folded up in his inside coat pocket.

Prosecutor Ralph Given asked Judge Scott to fix the bond at $2,000 each in the case of assault and highway robbery.

"I think," the court said, "that it would be better to raise it $1,000 and make it $3,000 in each case."
charles-smith-washington-1903-11-13.A2:
TRIED TO LYNCH NEGRO IN FRONT OF WHITE HOUSE.
Policeman Had Hard Struggle to Prevent Crowd at Washington From Stringing Up Robber.
Washington, Nov. 13.—Charles Smith, a negro, 18 years old, went into a lunchroom near the Treasury Department to-night, and at the point of a pistol compelled the clerk to give him the money in the cash drawer, $28 in all.

He then fled, but the clerk blew a whistle, and with Crossing Policeman Osborne gave chase. The negro turned on his pursuers and shot the officer in the thigh, causing a compound fracture.

Policeman C. M. Edwards then took up the pursuit, whereupon the negro again turned and fired, striking the policeman in the breast, but inflicting only a small bruise.

The negro was arrested.

When the police attempted to bring him from the alley in which he was captured, a crowd of several hundred persons made a rush for Smith, shouting, "Lynch him!"

The crowd seemed so determined that the police held the negro in the alley until re-enforced. The police pleaded with the crowd, but their entreaties were met with shouts of "Give him to us and we will finish him!"

Additional policemen finally arrived and the mob was forced back. The prisoner was taken to the station-house.
charles-smith-washington-1903-11-13.A3:
In Pursuit of Treasury Cafe Robber.
TOOK MONEY FROM CASHIER
Crowd Pursues Charles Smith, Who Is Captured by C. M. Edwards After Hard Fight.
Philip E. Steuart, cashier of the Treasury Cafe, at 1409 G Street north-west, was closing the cafe about 8:20 o'clock last night, when he was held up at the point of a gun and forced to deliver the late receipts, amounting to $28. The highwayman fled, and was pursued by several policemen, two of whom he shot as he ran. He was finally captured, and now two charges of assault with intent to kill and one of robbery are lodged against him. He proved to be Charles Smith, an eighteen-year-old negro, who was discharged from the Wednesday last.

Smith had been employed as a dishwasher in the cafe, which is owned by J. W. Bowling, for about three months, and was familiar with the habits of those employed there. He, therefore, knew that, at about this hour, Steuart would be alone, and would take the cash from the register just before locking up. Another custom was for Steuart to take a look through the kitchen to see that all was right before leaving.

Closing the Cafe.

Everything came off according to program last night, and Smith was watching the progress of events from outside. Steuart took out the cash and placed it in a little chamois bag, and then went to the kitchen for his final inspection. Just then he heard some one come in the front door. He returned to the front room to see who was entering after the lights had been turned down, and came face to face with a masked negro, who leveled a .38 caliber pistol at him and said: "I want that money."

With more than usual nerve Steuart pushed the gun aside, thinking that the man would weaken. Instead he again demanded the money, and Steuart was forced to give it up. Here the man turned and fled to the street, but Steuart followed him closely and blew his police whistle. The negro had turned west on G Street, and by the time he reached the corner of Fifteenth Street, Crossing Policeman G. W. Osburn, stationed at Fifteenth Street and New York Avenue, hearing the whistle, had also reached that corner. He tried to intercept the fleeing negro, and came near doing so, when Smith drew a revolver and fired at Osburn, who fell instantly, and so fast was he running that he rolled over after striking the pavement. It was afterward found that the ball had fractured the bone of the leg just above the knee, and the fall had made the fracture a compound one.

Crowd Follows Him.

By the time Smith turned into New York Avenue hundreds of pedestrians, who had witnessed the shooting of the policeman, and supposed him dead, had joined in the chase. Frank O. Parker, of 51 F Street northwest, was the closest to him, when Smith again whirled and fired point blank at Parker, but this bullet went wild. By this time Crossing Policeman C. M. Edwards, who is stationed at Fourteenth Street and New York Avenue, saw the runner and pursurers approaching and ran to meet them. He came up with Smith at the opening of the blind alley on the north side of New York Avenue half way between fourteenth and Fifteenth Streets, in the rear of the Oxford Hotel.

When Edwards was ten feet away, Smith fired his third and last shot, which struck Edwards just over the heart. That this shot was not instantly fatal is due only to the fact that Edwards had in his pocket a folded newspaper and two memorandum books, which broke the force of the bullet so that it only grazed the skin. Edwards was staggered, but did not abandon the pursuit for a moment, and a few feet within the alley came up with his man. There was a fierce struggle, in which Smith was disarmed, and overpowered. When the pistol was recovered it was found that it contained no more charges.

By this time, Policeman Bursey, and Crossing Policemen J. C. McCravey, from Fourteenth and G Streets, and J. P. Barrett, from Fourteenth and F Streets, had reached the scene, and it was well they did so, for the infuriated crowd was but a few feet behind them, and cries of "lynch him" and the like were freely heard, and it was only by a stiff fight that the negro was protected until the arrival of the patrol wagon. All the officers agree that, had the wagon been a moment later, it might have been impossible to protect him.

Smith's Rambling Tale.

At the stationhouse it was found that Smith still had the money on him, and that the mask he used was one of the napkins which he had taken from the restaurant while working there. He told a long and rambling story at headquarters this morning of a white man named Tommy Brown, a hibitue of the Union Mission, who had met him at the corner of Fourteenth and G Streets, had shown him the pistol, and proposed that he rob Steuart, for which was to get $10. Negro Narrowly Escapes Lynching Within Sight of White House at Washington
TWO POLICEMEN. WERE SHOT
When Officers Pursued the Colored Man He Turned and Fired—Mob Soon Gathers and Negro Is Beaten Unmercifully — Started in a Hold Up.
Washington, Nov. 14.—Charles Smith a negro desperado, narrowly escaped lynching last night within the shadows of the white house, and a race riot was barely averted within the hearing of President Roosevelt. Smith held up the cashier of a lunchroom near the treasury department at the point of a revolver and robbed him of $28, and, when pursued by a crowd and several policemen, he shot two officers.

A mob of 500 angry citizens gathered and unmercifully beat the negro, and demanded that he be lynched. some of the negroes in the mob protested against the treatment of Smith, and were promptly beaten.

For a few moments the national capital was in grave danger of being disgraced by a lynching and a race riot. There was no organized effort, however, to lynch the negro, who was locked up and his injuries treated.

Smith was employed as a dish washer in the Treasury cafe, 1409 G. street, but was discharged last Wednesday. Tonight he appeared at the cafe armed with a revolver and carrying a mask. Placing the mask upon his face, he entered the place and demanded money of the cashier, who was counting the receipts of the day. The negro's demand was reinforced by the revolver, and the cashier promptly handed over his funds.

As Smith left the cashier started in pursuit. He was joined by other citizens and the crossing policeman, G. W. Osburn and C. M. Edwards, stationed at the northeast corner of the treasury department.

Frank O. Parker, a bystander, outran the police and was close upon the heels of the negro, who suddenly turned and fired at him. The bullet missed Parker, but struck Osburn in the thigh. He fell to the ground with a groan, but Parker, Policeman Edwards, and a number of citizens continued in the pursuit, and Smith ran into an alley. As he entered he turned and fired again. This time the bullet struck Policeman Edwards in the breast. Edwards' life probably was saved by the bullet striking a bundle of papers in his coat pocket.

Other police then appeared on the scene, and Smith fired again, but this time the bullet went into the air, as those who were attempting to disarm him pushed his hand upward. The police disarmed Smith and in doing so administered a severe clubbing. A number of angry citizens also joined in the assault upon the negro.

There were cries of "Lynch him!" The situation was critical, and the three policemen, realizing a lynching was imminent, surrounded the negro and rescued him from the mob, escorted him to the patrol box, and summoned a patrol wagon.

While they were awaiting the arrival of the wagons with reinforcements, several negroes in the crowd noisily protested again the manner in which Smith had been treated, and several fights occurred. The negroes were outnumbered by the whites, and as matters were looking serious for them they disappeared.

Smith was taken to the station house and locked up. His two victims were conveyed to the emergency hospital, and upon being examined it was found that Osburn's leg was badly shattered, but Edwards was not wounded seriously, there being a red mark on his chest where the bullet struck.

CONVICTED OF MURDER.
Negro Found Guilty of Murder in First Degree for Brutal Killing of a White Boy Near Clarendon.
Clarendon, Dec. 11.—Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday of this week were consumed in the trial of John Bell for the murder of Winnie Gideon, a white boy 12 years old. F. E. Brown and Thomas & Lee represented the state, and M. J. Manning the defendant. The case was turned over to the jury about 5:15 p. m. and by 6 o'clock the jury brought in a verict of murder in the first degree.

Lyman Couch, an alleged accessory to the crime, testified he was with the defendant, John Bell, on the day of the murder, helping to unload cotton from a wagon into a cotton stall, and while doing this Winnie Gideon came up and climbed on the wagon and began helping to unload the cotton, and while in the wagon the defendant, Bell, took a pencil away from the little boy, who insisted that he give it back to him. Upon the negro's refusal to do so the child laid down on a plank near the wagon and began crying and threatened to tell his mother, whereupon the negro seized a stick and struck him across the back of the head, and then pushed him in the cotton stall and covered him with cotton, where he was found dead by one of the hands at the mill the next day.
clarendon-clarendon-1903-12-03.A7:
NEGRO HANGED
AT CLARENDON.
John Bell Pays Penalty for Murder of Boy-Protests Innocence to End.
Clarendon, Jan. 28.—John Bell, a negro, was hanged here this morning at 11:15 for the murder of Winnie Gideon, a white boy, on October 29 last, in Richland township, in the northern part of the county.

Sheriff Milwee sprung the trap at 11:15 and in three and a half minutes the physicians pronounced life extinct.

Bell never moved a muscle after the drop. His body was as motionless as a bag of sand. He protested his innocence to the very last, declaring that "an innocent child was being sacrificed." He asked all the negroes to "meet him in glory" and prayed fervently from the time the black cap was adjusted until the drop fell.

The crime for which Bell paid the penalty was the murder of a 12-year-old white boy. Bell and another negro were hauling cotton to a gin and the white boy went with them. Bell took a pencil from the boy, who cried and threatened to tell his mother. Bell thereupon seized a piece of rail and struck him back of the head, killing him almost instantly. The body was thrown into a stall in the gin and covered with seed cotton.
Norman Coach, a younger negro who was with Bell, testified to the manner of the killing and it was upon his evidence that the jury acted at the December term of court.

eddie-west-thunderbolt-1903-08-22.A1:
BULLET IN HIS BRAIN
NEGRO ARMED WITH PICKETT KILLED BY JULIAN BECKETT.
TRAGEDY AT THUNDERBOLT.
RAID ON GAMBLING GAME ENDED WITH A HOMICIDE.
Grinnell Ellis Wrenched a Picket From a Fence and Tried to Brain Mr. Beckett—Was Shot as He Was Advancing — Marshal Crawford Had Called Upon Mr. Beckett and Others to Assist in a Raid—Three Negroes Made Prisoners — Dead Man Was Well Known to Authorities.

While attempting to brain Mr. Julian Beckett with a picket at Thunderbolt at midnight last night Trinnell Ellis, colored, was shot through the head and killed. The shot was fired by Mr. Beckett, who had been called upon to assist in a raid on a house in which a crowd of negroes were gambling.

About midnight it was reported to Marshal Tom Crawford that half a dozen or more negroes were gambling in a shack near Bannon Lodge. The marshal organized a posse to raid the place, and Mr. Beckett was among those who answered the call. The shack was surrounded and the party closed in on the negroes, who were "skinning." As soon as the command to halt was given they scattered in every direction.

Ellis jumped from the house and wrenched a picket from the fence and started for Mr. Beckett, who was between him and liberty. As Ellis advanced on the young man he raised the picket to strike. Mr. Beckett said that in defense of his life he opened fire on the negro who fell in his tracks, the picket still in his hands.

Ellis may have been hit more than once, but a bullet through his head caused instant death. A number of shots were fired and three of the negroes who were in the house were made prisoners after the shooting. They were taken to the town jail where they are held for gambling.

Recorder L. W. Nelson immediately notified Coroner Keller of the tragedy. The coroner replied by telephone that he would leave the matter in the hands of the Thunderbolt authorities, but said he will make an investigation this morning. Inasmuch as there were eye witnesses to the homicide the coroner will probably decide than an inquest is unnecessary. In this event Mr. Beckett will be given a preliminary hearing by Recorder Nelson. Ellis was well known to the authorities at Thunderbolt and was at one time in the custody of the officers in the city. He was arrested several years ago with a white woman near Thunderbolt, and both were sentenced to the chaingang by Judge Norwood. Upon the promise of the woman to return to the North, from where she came, she was released, but the negro served out his sentence. The woman did not leave the city, but some time later committed suicide in a house near York lane and Price streets.
eddie-west-thunderbolt-1903-08-22.A2:
BULLETS FLEW FAST
TRINNELL ELLIS WAS SHOT TWICE AT THUNDERBOLT.
ANOTHER NEGRO WOUNDED.
WITH BULLET IN HIS ARM HE ESCAPED IN THE WEEDS.
Mr. Beckett Says Ellis Was Turning on Him With Picket When He Fired Fatal Shot—Marshal Crawfor Charges That First Shot Was Fired by One of the Negro Gamblers—Men Ran Into Coffee Weeds at Rear of House—Officer Fired Four Times and Winged One. Recorder Nelson Will Hold Preliminary Investigation To-day.

In the fusilade at Thunderbolt Saturday night that ended with the killing of Trinnell Ellis, colored, by Julian Beckett, eight shots were fired and a second negro was wounded.

Marshal Crawford learned yesterday that one of the four shots that he fired wounded a negro named Eddie West in the arm. West has not yet been made a prisoner. Joe Spaulding, Anderson Tyler, alias "Big One," and Isaac Brown are all held on a charge of having been engaged in a game of skin that was in progress when the raid was made.

Marshal Crawford was accompanied by Capt. Parker and Mr. Beckett, and was at the rear of the house when Ellis was killed. The marshal states that the negroes, with the exception of Ellis, escaped through a rear door. As they ran one fired at him, the lights were blown out and some four or five disappeared in a heavy growth of coffee weeds. The officer opened fire, and shot four times. One of the bullets wounded West, but the negro did not stop. Spellman and Tyler remained in the house, where they were found by the officer.

Ellis had gotten out of the front yard when shot by Mr. Beckett and fell in the road. The negro, Mr. Beckett says, pulled a picket from the fence and turned upon him, at the same time applying a vile epithet. The young man said it was then that he fired. The negro was wounded in the leg as well as in the head. He lived probably thirty minutes after the shooting, but made no statement. Coroner Keller went to Thunderbolt yesterday morning and decided to leave the matter in the hands of the authorities there. Mr. Beckett, who is connected with the Warsaw Ice and Light Company, was not locked up, and spent the day at the company's plant at Thunderbolt. He will be given a preliminary examination by Recorder Nelson this morning, and at the same time the cases against the three negroes under arrest will be heard. The body of the dead negro was turned over to his sister for burial.
eddie-west-thunderbolt-1903-08-22.A3:
BECKETT JUSTIFIED IN KILLING ELLIS.
Recorder Nelson Investigated Thunderbolt Tragedy.

The killing of Trinnell Ellis by Mr. Julian Beckett at Thunderbolt Saturday night was investigated by Recorder L. W. Nelson yesterday morning, and Mr. Beckett was exonerated.

The statements of Marshal Tom Crawford, Capt. Parker and Mr. Beckett were in accord with the facts given in the Morning News. Dr. McGee, who made an examination of the wounds, stated that the bullet had entered the negro's mouth and gone out at the back of the head. There was not the slightest conflict in the evidence, and the young man was promptly dismissed. It was shown that Ellis was a dangerous negro and was advancing upon Mr. Beckett with a pletet when the fatal shot was fired.

At the Mercy of Raging Waters.
St. Louis, June 10.—One half of East St. Louis is buried in the flood. Ten thousand persons are homeless and families are penned up prisoners in the garrets of their homes or on their roofs. They are without food and are crying for help. Two thousand people who sought refuge in the schools and churches and the plant of the St. Louis Syrup Refining Company are prisoners and suffering greatly. The break in the Illinois Central dyke came at 30 minutes after midnight. In five minutes a mighty maddened torrent was tearing through the large residence section in the eastern part of the city. The people, thousands of whom were sleeping, felt certain that the city was safe, but were warned by the blowing of train whistles and by the firing of riot guns. The property loss cannot be estimated. Many have not only lost all of their worldly possessions, but they are in dire need. The water stands from three to thirty feet deep all over the eastern half of the city. Houses are weakening and falling. The destruction seems complete. The flood came down upon the city from the southeast, this being a great pile of blackwater which had piled up against the city. At 8 o'clock this morning the flood had swept clear through to the river and the city lies under and unbroken stretch of rising, swirling torrents. East Broadway, the principal thoroughfare of East St. Louis, is crumbling away under the flood which is cutting through on the embankment from the southeast creeping down to the northern part of the city. At 8 o'clock the water had reached the high level of Broadway and was sweeping over the street. The destruction of Broadway will cut off all means of escape. It is conservatively estimated that thirty persons were drowned during the night. Other estimates are as high as 100.

Chief of Police Purdy of East St. Louis at 5 o'clock this morning sent an urgent appeal to the St. Louis authorities. Chief Purdy said 10,000 lives were in peril. Boats or anything that will float are urgently asked. Steps were taken to render all aid in the power of St. Louisans. Two negroes were shot and killed on the levee before the break last night. Ned Roberts, who had worked on the dyke several days, demanded his pay and threatened to break the dyke unless he was paid at once. Instantly seven men fired on him and the negro fell dead. Elijah Anderson, another negro, on the Illinois Central levee, refused to work and was killed by the guard. Theodore Day, colored, while trying to rescue some people was drowned as was the horse he was driving.

Relief Boats Assist.

Relief boats started from St. Louis for East St. Louis early this morning. By order of Park Commissioner Aull, the skiffs used for recreation on the park lakes were collected, to be sent out on a Wiggins ferryboat to the east side.

Congressman Wm. A. Rodenburg has issued an appeal for aid for the flood sufferers. Food, he says, is mostly needed and means must be had for delivering it to persons who are in upper stories of their homes or in box cars.

At 9 o'clock this morning the water was threatening the north and east sides, preserved temporarily by the Baltimore and Ohio railroad embankment, and had reached to the viaduct, only seven blocks east of the city hall. In this public building a foot and a half of seep water had already collected. All low points of the city are under water.

When the break occurred warnings were first sent through the Dexter addition by messengers, who discharged firearms, blew horns and shouted the news of the flood arrival. Lights gleamed in houses where the occupants had retired in confidence that the embankments would hold. Persons scantily attired emerged from their homes and in a few moments the whole populace of the low district, six miles in area, was fleeing to higher ground.

People Fly in Panic.

As the noise of the approaching flood was heard, the flight, at first a rapid retreat with more semblance of order, assumed a panic stage. All efforts to assure the inhabitants that there was sufficient time to escape unless a gap was washed through the embankment failed to convince them, and most of them fled without any effort to save property.

Messengers were sent to the main portion of the city, telling of the danger from the new point of attack and the greatest excitement prevailed. As the bottoms filled and the river gained a larger entrance, the terror in the business section of the city grew intense. It was all the greater because of the darkness and the fear that while guard was maintained in one direction the torrent would break through at another point and engulf the luckless inhabitants between two floods. By the thousands they began to desert their homes and run vainly up and down the streets seeking a place of succor.

Hundreds of families from the choicest residence portions of the city, carrying trunks, grips, bundles of clothing and valuables, began to cross Eads bridge toward St. Louis.

Refugees Scantily Clad.

Most of the refugees were scantily clad. Strong men carried aged women in their arms, followed by women with babies. Bare-footed children were in the procession, which continued steadily over the bridge. Hundreds of others sought protection in the second story of the public library building.

As the water encroached about it many dashed through the shallow overflow to find a more secure refuge. In terror of the rising tide of water, refugees in hundreds throng the streets, crowd the cars and bee-sech public officials for aid.

In the city hall alone 500 homeless persons, with such scant belongings as they had been able to seize on short notice, were assembled. Provisions for the time being were supplied them, and they were made as comfortable as possible in the Auditorium on the third floor.

All Business Suspended.

Business is totally suspended. The streets are filled with the almost panic-stricken inhabitants of the invaded districts. Women with children in arms, men carrying household furniture, horses, dogs and other remains of once comfortable domestic establishments, parade the streets. The common direction of all movement is toward the bridge, over which the refugees are hurrying to St. Louis.

At sunrise the bridge was practically the only means of crossing the river open to the throng. All traffic to East St. Louis from the west side was suspended and policemen turned back all who attempted the trip. The Eads bridge cars go to the west side of Cahokia creek viaduct where passengers dismount, walk over and take the cars at the east end. The viaduct is in a precarious condition and is not expected to stand long.

Thirty Reported Drowned.

ST. LOUIS, June 10.—The utmost confusion reigns in East St. Louis, and it is impossible to confirm any of the reports of drowning, which may aggregate fifty, and which may probably be much less. Congressman Rodenberg, who has charge of the patrol along broadway, which cuts the town in two east and west and leads to the Eads bridge, gives it as his opinion that the number will be about thirty. The only drownings coming under his personal observation were those of two women and a man who lost their lives near his post of duty.

Numerous drownings are reported among levee workers, who were caught asleep by the flood, but their number is not known.

All railroad and wagon communication with East St. Louis has been cut off. Only a limited number of pedestrians are allowed to cross the viaduct to East St. Louis. Refugees from East St. Louis are allowed to use the viaduct.

Telegraph and telephone communication is still intact. Although water has entered the first floors of the buildings occupied by the telegraph and telephone companies, the instruments have been elevated out of its reach and the managers say that they will maintain service to the last.

Six indictments against white citizens of Barbour County charging "white capping" were returned yesterday by the United States grand jury for the Middle District of Alabama, with a list of twenty-two indictments returned in a partial report to Judge Thomas G. Jones.

The indictments are against Jesse Green, Bufort McCall, Morgan Padgett, John Green, James Sanders and Richard Knowles, all citizens of Zeiglers postoffice, Beat 8, Barbour County. They are charged with violating Section 5508 of the Revised statutes of the United States, relative to conspiracy by two or more persons to injure, oppress, threaten, or intimidate any citizen in the free exercise or enjoyment of any constitutional privilege.

The indictments charge the men with having violated this section in the cases of Albert Barefield, Marion Shipman, Hillard Turner and Nancy Miles, negroes.

Jesse Green, Bufort McCall, Morgan Padgett, John Green and James Sanders were yesterday afternoon arraigned in open court.

At that time, it was indicated that all five men would plead guilty and ask for the mercy of the court.

There is not a bad face among the five men. All the men are rough and illiterate in appearance. Three of them are splendid specimens of physical manhood. They seemed to be awed by the solemnity of the court.

Judge Jones, presiding, stated to the prisoners the seriousness of the charge against them. He said that he understood that they considered themselves, not liable to federal prosecution on account of having been tried in the State courts for an assault and battery on one of the negroes, whom they are alleged to have "whitecapped."

Judge Jones informed the prisoners that the prosecution in the State courts for assault and battery could give them no good plea of former jeopardy. He told the men that if they wanted to, and knew they were really guilty, they could enter pleas of guilty. On the other hand if they desired a trial, he wanted to impress upon them that a fair and unbiased hearing would be given them.

One man said he would like to make a statement in reference to his position.

Judge Jones told him that if he intended to plead not guilty it would be best for him to make his statement to a lawyer.

"Just Naturally" Innocent.

"Well, Judge, I jés naturally ain't guilty," declared the prisoner. The others nodded approval.

"In that case," said the Judge, "I would advise you to engage a good lawyer and when you engage him, make a clean breast of the affair to him. He will know what is best for you to do."

Strike of the Telegraph Boys.

The story of the fight between George Gould, principal owner of the Western Union Telegraph Company, and A. J. Cassatt, president of the Pennsylvania Railroad, has been told in The Times-Dispatch. It will be recalled that one of the overt acts of Mr. Cassatt was to cut down the poles of the Western Union along the lines of the Pennsylvania Railroad system, involving a loss to Mr. Gould, as we have heard, of several million dollars. It is not surprising, therefore, that Mr. Gould should order a reduction of expenses in the operation of his extensive telegraph system, and in pursuance of that policy should have ordered a cut in the wages of the unorganized messenger boys from two cents for deliveries, and two and a half cents for calls, to a cent and a half for each delivery and each call. That is his own affair. The cut may be justifiable from his point of view. We do not undertake to dictate to any man how he shall conduct his business, or what wages he shall pay. It was Mr. Gould's right to cut wages, and it was the right of the messenger boys of Richmond to refuse to work at the reduced scale.

Mr. Gould also has the right to fill the places made vacant by the strike with negro men. APPEALING TO RACE PREJUDICE.

We confess that we were astounded to read in the editorial columns of the Richmond, Va., NEWS-LEADER, one of the most remarkable appeals to race prejudice that has ever appeared in the columns of any reputable journal. The heading, "Western Union Draws the Color-line" is in itself misleading, for this is just the opposite of what the corporation has done, even if we accept the NEWS-LEADER's own statements. This appeal appeared in the issue of the 15th inst., and under the rulings and decisions of the Hustings Court of this city, notably established in the boycott-case of the BAUGHMAN BROTHERS is a direct advocacy of the unlawful boycott, for it calls upon the southern business men and the white people of all kinds and classes to boycott the Western Union offices.

This advice is not only incendiary, but, if put in practice is unlawful. The Richmond, Va., NEWS-LEADER has recently given voice to some admirable statements on the race question and we are puzzled to know by what legerdermain process it has taken an another tack. It is said that an eel is somewhat remarkable, in that, if it is cooked at night, it will be raw by morning.

Our esteemed contemporary by its admirable article in reply to the vapors of the Richmond, Va., CHRISTIAN ADVOCATE had led the conservative colored citizens to hope that it had adopted a policy which would be observed and followed to the end of the chapter, or at least as long as the journal was under the present management. It was cooked then, but it is raw now. Certainly the editor who wrote the one article commeratory of the Negro could not have consistently written the article condemnatory of him. "It appears that the substitution of colored for white boys in the messenger service of the Western Union Telegraph Company is not a local matter peculiar to Richmond. East St. Louis Mob Gives Long Chase in Attempt to Lynch Joseph Erwin.
POLICEMAN HOLDS THEM BACK
Patrolman Mulqueeny Draws His Revolvers and Threatens to Shoot the First to Advance on Prostrate Negro.
Joseph Erwin, a negro, shot Edward Lawson, a one-armed white man, through the breast above the heart, after robbing him of $27 in money and his overcoat yesterday afternoon about 4:30. He also slightly wounded D. R. Bradley, a negro, in the back. Lawson is not expected to live.

A mob of several hundred persons chased the negro for a dozen blocks and finally into the arms of Policeman P. J. Mulqueeny, who had to draw both his revolvers to keep the crowd back. For half an hour, while awaiting the arrival of the patrol wagon Policeman Mulqueeny stood in the doorway of a saloon with his revolvers levelled on the crowd in order to keep it from getting at Erwin.

Lawson is 30 years old and came to East St. Louis yesterday morning with William Hall, 17 years old, from Mount Vernon, Ind. Yesterday afternoon they went to the raliroad yards in search of work. Near the old East St. Louis race track they came across Erwin and several boys, who were cleaning fish which they had caught in the slough. They watched them for a moment, when Erwin drew a revolver and told Lawson to throw up his hands.

Hall and the other boys ran when the negro drew the revolver. Erwin searched Lawson's clothes first, and, finding no weapon, turned his pockets inside out for money. He found $27 and then told Lawson to take off his overcoat, which he did.

As he handed it to the negro the latter pulled the trigger of his weapon, it is said. A 44-caliber bullet struck Lawson in the left breast, going through his ribs and lungs just above the heart and coming out on the right side.

Several of the boys, who had run a few hundred feet way turned to come back at the sound of the shot, but Erwin turned the revolver on them, inflicting a flesh wound in the back of D. R. Bradley, a negro boy.

Erwin then threw his revolver into the weeds and ran toward the heart of the city. The boys in the meantime had spread the story of the hold-up and shooting among the railroad men, half a hundred of whom followed the fleeing negro. This crowd was augmented every block.

At Tenth street and Tudor avenue the negro ran into the arms of Policeman P. J. Mulqueeny, who grabbed him and felled him when he tried to pass him. The mob surrounded the officer and shouted, "Lynch the negro."

Policeman Mulqueeny drew two revolvers, and telling the negro to march in front of him he turned to the crowd and called to them that the first man who approached would be shot. He walked the negro to Jackson's saloon, where he turned him over to several citizens, one of whom telephoned for the patrol wagon.

The news of the shooting spread quickly and the original mob was augmented by hundreds of men and boys. Ropes were brought and for awhile it looked as if the mob intended storming the saloon.

During this time Mulqueeny stood at the door of the saloon with his revolvers leveled, and threatened to shoot any who should attempt to gain entrance to the saloon. The negro, fearing that he would be lynched, cowered on the floor of the saloon and pleaded for his life.

The arrival of the police probably saved the negro from being lynched, as a number of the mob had made their way through rear yards and were ready to break into the rear of the saloon when the patrol wagon arrived.

An ambulance in the meantime had been summoned and conveyed Lawson to St. Mary's Hospital, where Doctor H. J. De Haan, attended him. He stated last night that Lawson's chances for recovery were very small.

Erwin was taken to the police station, where he was positively identified by Hall, Bradley and several others, who witnessed the hold-up. He denied his identity.

As a result of a quarrel between two cabmen early to-day Michael Lynch is dying in the New York Hospital with fourteen stab wounds in his abdomen and John Brown is locked up in the Tenderloin station, awaiting the outcome of the injuries he inflicted upon Lynch. It was by hard work of the police that Brown was saved from the hands of an angry crowd.

Lynch and Brown were stationed with their cabs outside the Haymarket dance hall, at Sixth avenue and Thirtieth street. A man and a woman appeared in the street and both men rushed toward them, offering their vehicles. Lynch took offense at Brown, who is a colored man, and both men forgot their prospective fares.

Blows followed profane language and Brown was getting the worst of the encounter when he is said to have pulled a knife from his pocket. The blade was long and slender, and with a dexterous underhand swing he thrust it into Lynch's body.

Time after time he plunged the blade into the man's side, and when Lynch fell to the sidewalk, yelling with pain, the negro is said to have leaped on top of him, continuing to use the knife. Those in the crowd which had gathered feared to go near the now infuriated man and it was not until Policeman Busweiller arrived that he was pulled from his victim.

Brown turned on the policeman and it was all Busweiller could do to hold him until the reserves came from the station-house half a block away. It took several policemen to drag the negro to a cell. The knife had to be torn from his grasp.

When he was no longer armed the crowd became boisterous. Half a hundred men were gathered at the corner, and Lynch still lay on the sidewalk, the blood streaming from his many wounds. The might infuriated them, and they made a rush at the negro. There were cries of "Lynch him! Kill him!"

The reserves surrounded their prisoner and fought off the crowd, but they might not have been successful had not the ambulance arrived to distract the attention of the crowd. Lynch was hurriedly lifted into the vehicle and hurried away to the hospital.

On the operating table it was found that Brown had used his knife fourteen times in a space not more than eight inches square. Several of the thrusts out into the intestines, and the doctors say there is little or no hope that the man can recover.

Brown is in a cell at the Tenderloin station and refuses to talk. There are several witnesses who say that Lynch provoked the attack and that Brown acted in self-defense. Others insist that the negro started the quarrel.

A NEW POSTAL OUTRAGE.
LIKE INDIANOLA CASE.
Negro Carrier Forced to Quit Service Under Penalty of Death.
[BY TELEGRAPH TO THE TRIBUNE.]ington May 7 - An outrage sim

Washington, May 7.—An outrage similar in detail to that which occurred at Indianola, Miss., was brought to the attention of the Postmaster General to-day by a telegram from Gallatin, Tenn., announcing that John C. Allgood, a colored rural free delivery letter carrier, while making his regular trip near Gallatin, was stopped by armed and masked men, and that he and his colored substitute carrier were warned not to continue in the service under penalty of death. Postmaster General Payne has suspended service on the route pending investigation, and if the reports of the affair are confirmed summary action will follow. The telegram, which was from Postmaster Swaney of Gallatin, read as follows:

Carrier rural route one, while making trip today, held up by masked men. Ordered not to make another trip. Advise.

Allgood was appointed only three weeks ago to succeed Allen F. Dillard, also colored, who was the first carrier on the route, and who, after serving less than two months, resigned. When asked why Dillard resigned, Postmaster General Payne said he did not know, but he could make a shrewd guess. He presumed it was "to avoid trouble."

Soon after the receipt of the above telegram a dispatch from W. F. Conger, special agent for rural free delivery, with headquarters at Nashville, was received. It read as follows:

Rural carrier No. 1, colored, Gallatin, Tenn., in an interview with me to-night, advises that he was stopped on route to-day by armed masked men, and his life threatened if he continued in service. Threat also applies to colored sub-carrier. Warned not to divulge cause of his removal, but to assign other reasons. No time allowed him to wait upon appointment of successor. Believing it hazardous, he will not serve route to-morrow unless assurances are given him that no violence will be committed. Please advise me what instructions will be issued in the premises. An immediate answer will be greatly appreciated.

SERVICE ON ROUTE SUSPENDED.

On receipt of Mr. Conger's message Mr. Payne, after ascertaining such facts as could be gleaned in the department regarding the appointment of Dillard and Allgood, telegraphed to Mr. Conger as follows:

Investigate fully case of John C. Allgood, rural free delivery carrier, who was stopped by armed masked men yesterday and his life threatened if he continued in the service, and report. In the mean time service on route will be suspended until your report upon the facts in the case is received.

To a correspondent of The Tribune the Postmaster General said this afternoon that he could not afford to take the responsibility of ordering Allgood to continue on his route when his life had been threatened, nor did he believe that the government could afford to send a detachment of soldiers to the scene to act as escort and protect the carrier from assault. Therefore he had suspended the delivery of mail on the route named until Special Agent Conger had finished his investigations. Should Allgood appear to have been unduly frightened or to have exaggerated the facts, the service would doubtless be resumed, but if the facts were as they appeared on the face of the advices thus far received the route would doubtless remain suspended indefinitely.

Mr. Payne further said that, under the law, the department had no option with regard to the appointment of rural delivery carriers, but was compelled to take the man certified by the Civil Service Commission. In this instance it happened that the three men whose averages were highest in their examination were colored.

Incidentally, Mr. Payne said that Nashville, from which the Gallatin route started, was the home of Senator Bate, and it has been suggested that his influence, when the matter is brought to his attention, may prove sufficient to enable him to guarantee that no violence will be attempted. The Gallatin route was only established on March 1, and, as stated above, Allgood is the second carrier who has attempted to perform his duties under the law, and is presumably the second man to be deterred therefrom by threats of violence. The Gallatin route is in the IVth Congress District, which is represented in the House by Morgan C. Fitzpatrick, of Hartsville.

It is said at the department that the penalties provided by law for such offences are covered in Sections 3,869 and 3,995, of the Revised Statutes. The former reads as follows:

Every person who wilfully and maliciously assaults any letter carrier who is in uniform while engaged on his route in the discharge of his duty as a letter carrier, and every person who wilfully aids or assists therein, shall for every such offence be punished by a fine of not less than $100 and not more than $1,000, or by imprisonment for not less than one year and not more than three years.

The other section provides that "any person who shall knowingly and wilfully obstruct or retard the passage of mail carrier shall for every such offence be punishable by a fine of not more than $100."

It is pointed out that the difference between these penalties hinges on the wearing of the uniform, and also that the word "assault," within the meaning of the law, contemplates just such an offence as that reported.

THE NEGRO AND THE MAILS.
A Negro Rural Free Delivery Carrier Held Up By Armed Masked Men in Tennessee.
Washington Cor. News and Courier.

Serious trouble broke out in a new place in the postoffice department last week. Postmaster General Payne received telegrams from postal officials in Tennessee, stating that John C. Allgood, a negro rural free delivery carrier at Gallatin, had been held up while performing his duties by masked men and told to leave the service at once, under threats of death.

Postmaster General Payne suspended the service on the route pending investigation. He looks upon the matter as very serious, as there are many negro carriers in the rural free delivery districts of the South, and a suspension of a large part of the service is possible if the white people maintain their present attitude.

Mr. Conger is the rural free delivery inspector for the State of Tennessee. The route on which the trouble occurred was put into effect by the department on the first of March, and there were five applicants under the civil service rules for appointment as carrier. The three men who stood highest in the examination were all negroes. The highest on the list, Allen Dilyard, received the appointment, as there was no option for the postoffice officials. Shortly afterwards he resigned his place and the second man on the list was appointed—John C. Allgood.

This case is regarded as more serious than the Indianola affair, because it involves the crime of holding up the mails and precipitates anew the race problem in the South. In speaking of the affair tonight, Postmaster General Payne says: "There are only two courses left open for the department: We must either suspend the rural free delivery service in those districts where the white people object to negro carriers, or we must send United States soldiers to protect these carriers in the performance of their duties. It would not be practical to give them a military guard, and, although no decision has been reached, the probable result will be a permanent suspension of the business in districts where such trouble occurs. After further investigation and report, the case in Tennessee will probably be referred to the department of justice."

This latest incident in Tennessee is regarded here as another important phase of the race problem in the South. Representative Gaines, of Tennessee, in whose district there are several negro rural carriers, explained the southern side of this question, by saying tonight that the women and children in the sparsely settled communities of the South, were afraid to have the negroes come to their houses to deliver the mail.

NO PLACE FOR COLOR LINE.
NO PLACE FOR COLOR LINE.

The Tennessee letter carrier has become an incident of national importance, says the Washington Post. Newspapers of every section are discussing him, with the intelligence one might have expected of them, respectively, and in due time he will be burning issue for lecturers, orators, and magazine writers. Meanwhile, we find southern comment more interesting than any other, and for the simple and sufficient reason that southerners only understand the situation and are competent to discuss it with authority. Of course, they disagree. The descendants of the old slave holding class have a great liking, not to say affection, for the negroes, whereas the descendants of the trader and overseer hold them in undying hatred and contempt—a feeling which the blacks cordially reciprocate. But we experience no difficulty in differentiating the two varieties, or in setting the proper value on their utterances.

A commentary which especially interests us, and which will serve to illustrate our point appears in a Memphis paper, the Evening Scimitar, conducted by Mr. A. B. Pickett, of that city. We quote a few specimen sentiments from an editorial article which appeared in its issue of the 8th instant:

"The white people of Memphis are as fully convinced of the recessity for drawing the color line in the proper places as any southerners could be, but they are not childish or malicious in the matter. They bear the negro no ill will and are pleased rather than disgruntled to see him getting on in the world. Certain it is that they would never think of objecting to a well conducted and respectably dressed negro acting as a letter carrier.

"We do not believe that the responsible white citizens of Sumner county differ in this respect from the white people of Memphis. In our opinion, it will be found, upon investigation, that the interference with Carrier Algood is chargeable to a class of whites who rarely write or receive letters, and who may have wanted some particular white man to get the job that the negro won in open competition.

"Next to the professed negrophiles, who contend that the black man is the equal of the white in all respects except opportunity, and should be so acknowledged, the worst trouble breeders are those southern whites who would put the negro off the earth if they could. They are almost all of the class of whites who have had no experience with the negro in the capacity of an employer, for the very good reason that no negro in his senses would work for them." This is, in all important respects, precisely the view of the matter taken expressed on more than one occasion within the past few days. Of course, we do not consider Algood's certificate from the civil service commission as a matter of the slightest consequence, holding that the examination could not possibly disclose any qualification worthy of respectful notice, and insisting that the postoffice officials should be left free to choose their own subordinates. The fact remains, however, as the Scimitar declares, that there is no place for the color line in such cases as this, and that those who try to draw it are not representative of the better class among the whites. The colored man, all other things being equal, makes quite as efficient and acceptable a letter carrier as any white man whose aspirations can be satisfied by such employment, and he is as little likely to give offense to well bred people in the discharge of his duties. Indeed, our observation teaches us that the negro is disposed to take a pride in occupations of this kind and to conduct himself with the most exemplary and commendable propriety.

It is a great pity this perilous and lamentable question should have been revived. The agitation will serve no useful purpose, or bring to the surface any wholesome agencies.

IN SELF-DEFENSE.
Portsmouth, R. I., Farmer Obliged to Kill an Ugly Negro.
Newport, R. L., Feb. 20.—A discharged negro farm hand named Potter, after making a target, this morning, of his former employer, Isaac Chase, a well-to-do farmer of Portsmouth, came dead by Chase, as the latter claims, in self-defense.

After being shot at by the negro, this morning, Chase tried to get some of the town or county authorities to come to Portsmouth and arrest Potter before he could leave the island. But no officer was available, so when the negro re-appeared at the farm and again became threatening, Chase was obliged to take the law into his own hands. An hour or two after the fatality a deputy sheriff went to Portsmouth and Chase gave himself up at once and was locked up in the county jail. The body of the negro was searched and he was found to have been well armed.

Although Potter had been employed on the farm for nearly three years, very little is known of his antecedents, nor even his first name. For the past month he had several altercations with his employer, which culminated in his not only being discharged but being warned never to set foot on the farm again.

It was thought that he had left the island, when he suddenly appeared, this morning, as Mr. Chase and his daughter were driving out in a sleigh. A few words had passed between the men when Potter suddenly whipped out a revolver and fired directly at Mr. Chase. Although he stood almost beside the sleigh the bullet went wild.

Mr. Chase hastily drove to the nearest telephone and notified Sheriff Anthony of Potter's attempt on his life. He urged the sheriff to come out and arrest Potter before the latter could leave the island, but the sheriff told him to see the town sergeant and get him to follow up the negro.

Mr. Chase hunted around town for an hour or more trying to find the sergeant and finally ascertained that he had gone away. He then went back home to dinner, rather apprehensive that Potter might reappear before he could call up the sheriff again.

About 2 o'clock, Potter was seen coming down the road. Mr. Chase, arming himself with a shot gun, well loaded with buck shot, started out of the house. Just what was said is not known, but the result was that Chase fired the contents of one barrel at the negro and Potter dropped dead in his tracks.

PORTER INQUEST HELD
Coroner Hicks Holds Inquiry Into the Shooting of the Colored Man at Portsmouth.
Coroner George E. Hicks conducted his inquest into the death of Charles Porter, the colored man alleged to have been killed by Isaac Chase, at the Portsmouth town hall, yesterday afternoon. The inquest lasted three hours, the examinations being particularly searching.

F. F. Nolan was present to represent the dead man and his friends, and William P. Sheffield, Jr., and Max Levy were present in the interests of Mr. Chase. Mrs. Chase also told her story with great effort, for she was in a highly nervous state.

A number of witnesses were called, all of whom testified substantially to the events of the fateful morning, as published, and all agreeing as to the facts in the case.

Isaac Chase told his story in detail, following incident after incident, from the first appearance of the man in the yard about 9:30, until Chase gave himself up. He said Porter claimed he, Chase, had disgraced his, Porter's, name, and that he, Chase, denied this. He said that in the yard when the witness was uncovering his horse, Porter stood close by and was working his hand about his clothes, so that he feared a razor. When he did this at the gate he thought a revolver was drawn. The story of the negro's trip up the road and return to the house was told, and then he said that while waiting for the officers he feared damage to his family and property, and with his rifle kept showing himself to the man, so that it would be realized he was on watch.

When the man went way up the road Chase said he even went out in the road. He denied that there were any grievances, and said he had not seen the man until that morning since he left in August, three or four years ago, neither had he heard from him. When Porter was on the farm Mr. Chase said he seemed to be "a little off," and declared that there was something on the wood pile, but Mr. Chase said he did not consider him insane.

The other witnesses called were Samuel Carter, George A. Carter, Minot A. Steele, Mrs. Chase, Fillmore Coggeshall, Frank Paquin, Augustus Chase and C. Woodman Chase.

Clarendon, June 25.—Shortly after midnight last night a mob of about fifty men called at the residence of Deputy Sheriff John Black and demanded the keys to the jail. The men are supposed to have been the friends and neighbors of John Coburn, the white man who sustained serious injuries at the hands of a negro named Jack Harris.

Sheriff Milwee readily agreed to let them into the jail and led the way, requesting them to choose a committee who should search the jail for the negro.

Mr. Milwee congratulated himself that he had outwitted the mob; for, fearing that something like a lynching would be attempted, he had given the negro into the custody of William Swift. Mr. Swift had conducted the prisoner to a barn that Sheriff Milwee had just built and there they were, in fancied security, while the mob were going through the jail. But it is now known that while the larger part of the mob were making this advance on the jail, another part were hot on the trail of the negro and his guard. It is not known how they knew the whereabouts of the men, but about the time the larger body of men were cursing their luck and departing from the jail, apparently convinced that they could not secure their man, that night at least, the other party had found Mr. Swift and his prisoner, had furnished good proof that it would be useless to try to save the negro, and were leading him away to find a convenient place to string him up.

Beaumont, Texas. February 5.—A ripple of excitement was created here this afternoon when it became noised that there had been a serious development of labor troubles at Sour Lake between the whites and blacks working on a pipe line from that field to the station on the railway.

The thing came up over a note sent day before yesterday by one of a number of white men there and handed to Mr. Will Kinsley, son of Contractor John Kinsley, who is constructing a pipe line from Sour Lake this way. The note stated that the negroes must leave there by yesterday at noon or trouble could be expected and the note intimated that the negroes would either be driven away or killed outright.

The note was signed "WE."

The colored employees, twenty-five in number, left yesterday and most of them are now in Beaumont.

This story comes from one of them and he states that he can not see the motive for it. He insists that the negroes have been receiving $15 a week straight and that the white men are getting $2 a day. He thought that if the negroes were working for less there might be some excuse, but he could hardly see the justice of it when the negroes were getting more wages. He says that twenty-five came to this city, all that were affected by the notice.

Mr. John Kinsley, the contractor, is in Beaumont, and has been making an effort today to get the men to return, but the one seen by the reporter said that his hide was a little too thin to withstand harsh treatment and the others were of the same opinion. He did not care to give his name for the reason that it might go hard with him.

Mr. Kinsley has not given out yet just what he proposes to do about it.

New Orleans, January 11.—A special to the Picayune from Summit, Miss., says:

News reached here today that the house of Squire Williams, colored, living about two miles west of Johnston Station, was burned by white caps last night. The negro was ordered to leave his premises some weeks ago by posted notice of the white caps, the first of January being the limit.

After consulting with some of his friends and some prominent citizens, he concluded that he would stay on the place, especially as he had bargained to buy it and had already made some improvement on the property. After burning the Williams house the marauders went to the house of Sam Caruth, in the same neighborhood and discharged their fire arms on his premises, evidently to intimidate his colored tenants. Sheriff Laggatt and Deputy Holmes are on the ground and will do their best to apprehend the depredators.

Dublin, Ga., Oct. 7.—Several gentlemen from Wilkinson county were in the city yesterday afternoon, and told of a street fight which occurred at Toombsboro Sunday night last, which, though bloodless, was exciting.

Recently the Town Council of Toombsboro passed an ordinance prohibiting crowds from congregating on the streets after 9 o'clock at night. Sunday night Marshal Rickerson found a number of negroes standing on the corner of one of the streets and ordered them to disperse. Instead of doing so, they pulled pistols and began shooting at him. DEADLY FIGHT IN TUNNEL CLASH BETWEEN NEGROES AND A POSSE AT FLUSHING, O. Marshal Shot Dead and a Colored Man Mortally Wounded-Wholesale Lynching Feared.
WHEELING, W. Va., Oct. 23.—John G. Elliott, marshal, is dead, and William Smith, colored, is dying as the result of a clash between officers and a mob of angry negro laborers and foreigners at Flushing, O. The fight took place in the tunnel of the Baltimore & Ohio Railroad at Flushing shortly after 10 o'clock to-night. Three of the gang are surrounded in a cabin by a posse of citizens, and a lynching is feared.

About 10 o'clock to-night Marshal Elliott was called to quell a disturbance in the streets caused by the negro. The officer cautioned them that a repetition would mean arrest, and two of the men assaulted him. Marshal Elliott ran for reinforcements, and when he returned the men had disappeared, but were tracked to the tunnel, where they had fortified themselves. Elliott led an attack, and fought the gang hand to hand, but a bullet pierced his heart and he fell dead in his tracks. The deputies removed his body from the tunnel and succeeded in capturing six of the men. The others fled. Two blacks and one foreigner were located in a lonely cabin at midnight. They met a demand for surrender with a volley of lead. The place is being held by the posse until the Belmont county officers, who are hurrying to the scene, arrive.

HONORS WERE EVEN
An Exciting Pitched Battle Occurred at Fort Riley.
Almost Like Real War - A Battery Was Captured with a Rush by Cavalry, but Soon After Re-taken by a Brilliant Ne-gro Infantry Charge.
Fort Riley, Kan., Oct. 24.—There was a pitched battle Friday seven miles northeast of the maneuver camp and it came about as close to the real thing as is possible with blank cartridges. It was good to look upon, better to be in and full of infantry dash and the touch and go of cavalry work.

The Browns, under Gen. Barry, represented a force advancing from the north. The Blues, under Gen. Bell, having been pushed out on a reconnoissance were attacked at once by the Browns and the resultant mix-up constituted a "contact of opposing forces of all arms." Gen. Barry's force, which marched out Thursday evening and endured a chilly bivouac, was forbidden by the conditions of the problem to march forward before 10:20 a. m. Gen. Bell left his camp at 7:30 a. m. and by the time Gen. Barry was privileged to start was close upon him and ready for operations.

As soon as the Browns moved out Col. Duncan, leading the Sixth infantry, the advance of Gen. Bell's force, charged home on their left flank, rolling it up and driving it back toward the center. Two troops of cavalry were quickly put out of action by Col. Duncan, who then swung in close upon the rear of the Browns and captured their entire baggage train. So far the battle was all for the Blues, but Gen. Barry's turn was coming, and his right came down on the Blue left in a fashion to make the latter gentlemen wonder why they had ever gone into the war business.

While his infantry poured in a heavy fire from the ridges, a squadron of the Tenth cavalry moved up a ravine close to the left of Gen. Bell's position and then, climbing a hill and peering over the crest Capt. Johnson beheld Gen. Bell and his entire staff riding but a short distance away. Gen. Barry, who was close up, ordered Capt. Johnson to charge and capture Gen. Bell, and if possible the Twentieth field battery, which was just in front. Johnson ordered the charge and in an instant he and his colored troopers were over the summit of the battery. The guns turned loose for a few shots that would have laid out many of Johnson's men and then it was all over. On a dead run Capt. Johnson with his troopers was in among the guns, and the battery was captured.

Without halting after dashing through the battery Capt. Johnson tore on after Gen. Bell, but here he failed and lost his life for the day. Between him and the prize he sought was a rank of men of the same color as his own, the boys of the Twenty-fifth infantry. Just as Johnson seemed to be swinging in on his prize, a line of dark faces rose in front and volley after volley was poured almost into him and his men.

The Twenty-fifth then rushed forward to a counter charge, recapturing the battery and then, coming down on the far side of the crest, they carried at the point of the bayonet the Nineteenth battery of Gen. Barry's force that had just come up. The guns were wheeled like lightning on the Twenty-fifth, but the colored men with loud cheers and firing with wonderful rapidity, charged along the hill and there was nothing that could stop them. The battery was theirs and they held it. While this charge was taking place Col. Lincoln's Fifty-first Iowa, which is in all things highly praised by the military critic, came forward on a ridge parallel to that along which the Twenty-fifth was charging and became hotly engaged with the support of the battery that had been taken by the Twenty-fifth. There is a grim earnestness in the fighting of the Iowa regiment that makes it an important factor no matter what the opponent pitted against it.

They came plunging down the hill, crossed a ravine and ascended the hill on the farther side just in time to meet an attack that Gen. Barry was sending in upon the Blue center. It was hot enough for anybody and the Iowa boys were given all they could do. A part of the Twenty-fifth came out to aid them, but Gen. Barry had the preponderance of force and made a vicious battle.

Iowa was soon overmatched, although she still hung on and the Nebraska and Missouri regiments sent up aid. Gen Barry was not to be denied, however, and his men came on steadily, pouring in a fearful file that would have been woefully destructive of life in an actual fight. The fight was at its hottest and the men were pressing closer when Col. Wagner, the senior umpire, sounded the recall and the battle closed.

NEGRO WHO COMMITTED RAPE LYNCHED AT WHIGHAM.
WHITE GIRL HIS VICTIM.

WAS HANGED AND RIDDLED.
Particulars of the unfortunate affair which happened near Whigham on Saturday have at length leaked out. William Williams, a negro who had been employed at the place of a Mr. Harrell four miles north of Whigham, was discharged Saturday morning. Mr. Harrell himself left early in the day for a point several miles away, to attend court. His little 7-year-old daughter was playing in the lot some distance from the house, about 8 o'clock, when she was attacked by the negro Williams. Her screams brought assistance from the house, and the negro fled.

A small posse, in charge of an uncle of the girl's, caught Williams soon afterward. They knew that an effort would be made to lynch the negro, and so decided to keep him secluded in the woods until nightfall, when they would bring him into town and slip him over to the jail at Bainbridge.

This plan went well until its last stage. Mr. Harrell and one other guard had proceeded to within a mile of Whigham when they were met about 8 o'clock Saturday night by a mob of some seventy-five men, who immediately relieved them of their burden.

The story runs rapidly from here. Williams was strung up to a tree and his body literally torn to pieces by bullets of every description.

Postmaster Quinn of Whagham was foreman of a coroner's jury that held an inquest over the body. No evidence was discovered against any man who belonged to the mob, though it seems that its ranks must have been filled from people out in the country. All the residents of Whigham were reported to have been in their accustomed places at the time the lynching occurred.
