Two Whites and Two Negroes Said to Have Been Too Zealous in Politics—Policeman Shoots a Negro Boy.
Advertiser Bureau.
Considerable surprise to the public and much consternation among the local postoffice employees was experienced this morning when it became known that four of the employes, two white and two colored, had been removed by Postmaster P. D. Barker. They are:

Benjamin B. Cox, white; foreman of distribution.

James T. Peterson, colored, foreman of letter carriers.

George B. Crane, white; clerk.

Clarence Allen, colored; letter carrier.

Postmaster Barker stated that the only information he could give was that the order had come to him from the Postoffice Department at Washington to discharge the employes named, it being alleged that they had violated the Civil Service Rules. What these violations were he did not say. He qualified this, however, by remarking that the investigation was from the head and not from this end of the department.

Benjamin B. Cox, who stepped down and out last night, is one of the most widely known citizens of Mobile. For eighteen years he had been connected with the local postoffice and he was ever pleasant to those with whom he had dealings.

James T. Peterson, the foreman of carriers, had also been connected with the local office eighteen years and although a colored man, had, by his uniform courtesy and deportment, acquired a large number of friends among the white residents of Mobile. He was looked upon as a fixture in the carrier department.

George B. Crane had only been in the postoffice two years, yet he, too, had won friends.

Clarence Allen, during his fifteen years as a letter carrier made for himself friends among the white people on his route by his polite address and promptness in performing his duties.

A dispatch from Washington explains the removals as follows:

"Inquiry at the Postoffice Department elicited the information that three employes of the postoffice at Mobile were removed June 26. B. B. Cox and James T. On the morning of August 17. J. R. Parker, John T. Parker, Rube Parker, Will Stafford, Clyde Stafford, J. H. Harrison (school teacher), S. W. McKinney, W. R. Clampit, Will England, Lee Bridges and Charles Blake, all white, and most of them well to do planters of Poinsett county, entered the sawmill belonging to Davis and Hodges, which is operated exclusively by negro labor, and ordered the negroes from the mill, threatening them with violence if they did not leave at once. Davis and Hodges think it is the work of some personal enemies, or grudge that some of the citizens have against them, as no other negroes were bothered, and the community is thickly populated with negroes. Convicted of Whitecapping.
The jury in federal court at Helena in the celebrated Poinsett county whitecapping cases returned a verdict, finding three of the defendants guilty, as charged. The remaining twelve were discharged. The convicted men were Reug Hoges, William Clampitt and Wash McKinney. All three were recommended to the mercy of the court by the jury. These arrests grew out of alleged intimidation of negro laborers at a saw mill, it being charged that the white men threat ened the negroes with death should they fail to leave the community.
wynne-wynne-1903-08-17.A27:
Convicted Ringleaders.
Helena, Ark.—For/the first time in the history of this section white men have been convicted in the federal court of white capping Negroes. Fifteen of the most prominent citizens of Poinsett county had been indicted for compelling Negroes to quit work at a sawmill, white men wanting their places. The jury convicted Reuben Hodges, Wm. Clampit and Wash McKinney, ringleaders.

Men Terrorized Negroes Are Sentenced in Arkansas. Helena, Ark, March 30.—Federal Judge Trieber last week passed sentence upon the three Pointsette county whitecappers, convicted in the federal court of conspiracy to intimidate Negro workmen at the saw mill of Davis & Hodges, at Whitehall, in Pointsette county. Reuben Hodges and William Clampit were given a year and a day in the Atlanta penitentiary and a fine of $100 each. and Wash McKinney was sentenced to sixty days in the Lee county jail and a fine of $100.
